name: International Business
notes: Official 2026-27 FBLA International Business guideline (national text in the PA FBLA copy, updated August 2026: https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/26-27-International-Business-PA.pdf): teams of 1 to 3, each member takes a 100-question, 50-minute objective test (scores averaged), and the top 15 teams give a 7-minute interactive role play. Test knowledge areas (items): Fundamental Economic Concepts (20), The Nature of Business (20), Economic Systems (20), Impact of Government (5), Business Law: import/export law and customs regulations (5), Global Trade (30). This bank was written before that guideline was found, so its subs use standard international business areas and over-weight trade finance and logistics; the economics and economic-systems areas still need questions. Group is set to case as requested.

questions.q: A U.S. software firm's home market is saturated and grows about 1 percent a year, but its board wants 15 percent annual growth. Which motive for going global best fits?
choices: Market-seeking motive: access new customers in faster-growing foreign markets
Resource-seeking motive: secure lower-cost raw materials abroad
Efficiency-seeking motive: consolidate production in a low-cost country
Strategic-asset-seeking motive: acquire a rival's patents
questions.explain: Market-seeking firms expand to reach new demand when the home market is mature. The other motives are real but do not solve a demand-growth problem.

questions.q: Country X can make 10 tons of wheat or 5 tons of cloth per year. Country Y can make 4 tons of wheat or 8 tons of cloth. Which statement is correct?
choices: X has a comparative advantage in cloth because it makes more cloth per year
Y has an absolute advantage in wheat because it can grow wheat on less land
X has a comparative advantage in wheat, and Y has one in cloth
Both countries should produce only wheat because wheat is the larger output
questions.explain: X gives up 0.5 tons of cloth per ton of wheat and Y gives up 2 tons, so X has the comparative advantage in wheat. Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, not total output.

questions.q: Which trade agreement replaced NAFTA in July 2020?
questions.explain: USMCA (called CUSMA in Canada) took effect July 1, 2020, and replaced NAFTA among the United States, Canada and Mexico.

questions.q: A government limits imports of bicycles to 10,000 units a year and blocks any shipments above that amount. This is an example of a(n):
questions.explain: A quota is a quantity limit. A tariff taxes the good rather than capping how many can enter.

questions.q: Which tariff is charged as a percentage of the good's declared value?
questions.explain: Ad valorem means according to value. A specific tariff is a fixed amount per unit, and an embargo is a complete ban on trade.

questions.q: Which exchange rate applies to currency delivered immediately, typically within two business days?
questions.explain: The spot rate is for near-immediate settlement. A forward rate is agreed today for a future date.

questions.q: In the 4Ps of the marketing mix, the P that is not product, price or place stands for:
questions.explain: The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion. Positioning is a strategy concept, not one of the four Ps.

questions.q: A U.S. construction firm's agent pays $5,000 in cash to a foreign official to win a contract. Which U.S. law governs this payment?
questions.explain: The FCPA prohibits paying foreign officials to obtain or keep business, including payments made through agents. The antitrust statutes address competition, not bribery.

questions.q: A U.S. running-shoe brand is positioned as fast and affordable in Canada. The same message reads as cheap in Japan, where buyers equate price with quality. What is the best explanation?
choices: Culture shapes how buyers read price and quality signals, so positioning must be localized
Japanese tariffs make affordable products impossible to import
Canadian consumers have higher incomes, so the message fits there
Hofstede's power distance is too high for any advertising to work
questions.explain: Cultural cues about what low price signals determine how a message lands, so the positioning has to be adapted. Tariffs and incomes do not explain how the message is read.

questions.q: In a PESTEL scan, a target country passes a new national data-privacy law that affects how foreign firms store customer data. Which category does this belong to?
questions.explain: Laws and regulations fall under the Legal factor of PESTEL. Data handling affects technology, but the source of the constraint is the law.

questions.q: Which framework compares a firm's internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats before entering a foreign market?
questions.explain: SWOT pairs internal factors (strengths, weaknesses) with external ones (opportunities, threats). Porter's five forces looks only at industry structure.

questions.q: A target market has high per-capita income, slow population growth and a rapidly aging population. Which PESTEL category most directly captures the aging population?
questions.explain: Demographic trends such as age structure are Social factors. Income levels would be Economic.

questions.q: Which principle explains why two countries can both gain from specializing and trading, even when one country is more efficient at producing everything?
questions.explain: Comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost, so trade still benefits both sides even when one country has an absolute advantage in every good.

questions.q: Which statement best defines a free trade area?
choices: Members remove tariffs among themselves but keep their own external tariffs
Members adopt a common external tariff and free movement of labour
Members use one currency and one central bank
Members set quotas on all imports from outside the group
questions.explain: In a free trade area, internal tariffs are removed but each member sets its own tariffs on outside countries. A customs union adds the common external tariff.

questions.q: Which stage of economic integration has a common external tariff, free trade among members, and free movement of labour and capital, but no harmonized economic or monetary policy?
questions.explain: A common market adds free movement of factors of production to a customs union. A customs union covers goods only. An economic union also harmonizes economic and monetary policy.

questions.q: A country exports $220 billion of goods and services and imports $260 billion. Net primary income is +$10 billion and net transfers are -$5 billion. What is the current account balance?
questions.explain: Goods and services balance is -40, plus net income of +10 gives -30, then net transfers of -5 give -35.

questions.q: Under the Heckscher-Ohlin model, a country with abundant skilled labour will tend to export:
questions.explain: Heckscher-Ohlin predicts a country exports goods that intensively use its abundant factor. Abundant skilled labour points to skill-intensive exports.

questions.q: A tariff cut lowers the price of a U.S. product in a foreign market, but the foreign currency depreciates 10 percent against the dollar. Which is the most accurate description of the net effect on U.S. price competitiveness there?
choices: Competitiveness improves for certain, since both changes lower the local price
Competitiveness falls for certain, since currency moves always outweigh tariffs
Ambiguous: the tariff cut helps, but the weaker currency raises the local price
Competitiveness is unchanged, since the two changes always cancel out exactly
questions.explain: A weaker local currency means buyers need more of it to cover a dollar price, which offsets part or all of the tariff saving. The net effect depends on the size of each change.

questions.q: Which argument for trade protection is most consistent with the infant industry concept?
choices: Protecting mature industries from competition for permanent job security
Temporarily protecting a new domestic industry until it can compete
Imposing tariffs to raise government revenue from all imports
Banning imports to conserve foreign exchange reserves permanently
questions.explain: The infant industry argument is temporary protection for a new industry expected to become competitive. Permanent protection of mature industries is not the concept.

questions.q: Which WTO mechanism settles trade disputes through a binding, rules-based process?
questions.explain: Disputes go to panels under the Dispute Settlement Body, and adopted rulings bind the parties. The Trade Policy Review Mechanism only monitors policies. Since December 2019 the Appellate Body has had no members, so a losing party can stall a panel ruling by appealing it.

questions.q: Which U.S. trade agreement covers the United States, the Dominican Republic and several Central American countries?
questions.explain: CAFTA-DR is the Central America-Dominican Republic Free Trade Agreement with the United States.

questions.q: What is the group of European Union countries that have adopted the euro as their currency called?
questions.explain: The eurozone (euro area) is the EU members that use the euro: 21 of 27 since Bulgaria joined on January 1, 2026. Schengen covers border-free travel, EFTA is a separate bloc of non-EU countries, and the EEA links the EU single market to three of them.

questions.q: Which regional bloc includes Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines?
questions.explain: ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, promotes economic and political cooperation in Southeast Asia. Mercosur and the Pacific Alliance are Latin American blocs, and the GCC groups Gulf states.

questions.q: Which principle requires a member to extend any trade advantage it gives one trading partner to all WTO members?
questions.explain: Most-favoured-nation treatment makes non-discrimination the default among WTO members. National treatment concerns how imports are treated after they enter.

questions.q: What does the acronym WTO stand for?
questions.explain: The World Trade Organization is the international body that sets rules for trade among nations.

questions.q: A U.S. exporter ships $40,000 of machine parts to Germany. Which filing reports the shipment to the U.S. government for export control and trade statistics?
questions.explain: EEI is filed electronically through the Automated Export System when any Schedule B line is worth more than $2,500 or an export licence is required. The other documents go to the buyer, the carrier or foreign customs.

questions.q: Which document certifies where goods were produced and is often needed for preferential tariff treatment?
questions.explain: A certificate of origin states the country where goods were made, which determines whether trade agreement rates apply.

questions.q: A U.S. exporter ships machinery and wants the buyer's bank to release the shipping documents only when the buyer pays, without any bank guaranteeing payment. Which payment method fits?
questions.explain: In a documentary collection (documents against payment), banks hand the documents to the buyer only on payment, so the exporter keeps control of the goods without the bank guarantee or cost of a letter of credit. Cash in advance is paid before shipping.

questions.q: Which payment method gives the exporter the strongest payment guarantee, because a bank commits to pay on compliant documents?
questions.explain: An irrevocable letter of credit is the bank's own promise to pay once the seller presents compliant documents. Documentary collection involves no such bank commitment.

questions.q: Under a letter of credit, which bank is obligated to pay the seller once compliant documents are presented?
choices: The issuing bank or a confirming bank
The advising bank, even if it has not confirmed
questions.explain: The issuing bank (for the buyer) or a confirming bank that adds its own promise must pay against compliant documents. An advising bank only passes the credit on to the seller unless it also confirms it.

questions.q: A country charges a compound tariff of $0.50 per kilogram plus 5 percent of customs value. An importer brings in 2,000 kg of cheese valued at $10,000. What is the total duty?
questions.explain: The specific part is 2,000 kg x $0.50 = $1,000 and the ad valorem part is 5% of $10,000 = $500, so the duty is $1,500. A compound tariff combines a per-unit (specific) duty with a percentage-of-value (ad valorem) duty.

questions.q: A country allows 50,000 imported cars a year at a 5 percent tariff and charges 40 percent on any cars above that amount. Which policy is this?
questions.explain: A tariff-rate quota combines a lower in-quota tariff with a higher out-of-quota tariff. A pure tariff applies one rate to all units.

questions.q: A country imposes a special duty on imports sold below fair value that injure its domestic producers. What is this duty called?
questions.explain: Antidumping duties offset sales below normal value. Countervailing duties offset foreign government subsidies.

questions.q: Which nontariff barrier requires products to meet specific technical, labelling or safety standards that favour domestic producers?
questions.explain: Technical barriers to trade are standards and conformity rules that can be used to protect domestic producers, even when they are not meant as tariffs.

questions.q: Which is an example of an export subsidy?
choices: A tariff that raises the price of imported steel
A government grant that cuts a firm's cost of shipping goods abroad
A quota that caps imported textiles each year
A licence requirement for exports of dual-use goods
questions.explain: An export subsidy lowers the cost of selling abroad. Tariffs, quotas and licence requirements restrict imports or exports rather than support them.

questions.q: A U.S. importer's commercial invoice shows a $50,000 FOB price at the foreign port of export. Under U.S. customs transaction-value rules, which amount is generally the basis for duty?
choices: Price including ocean freight and insurance
The buyer's resale price in the United States
questions.explain: U.S. transaction value is the price actually paid or payable and excludes international freight and insurance, so the FOB price is the base. Many other countries, such as EU members, value imports CIF instead.

questions.q: Which statement about the Harmonized System (HS) is correct?
choices: HS codes identify only the country where the goods were made
Each importer assigns its own codes, so they vary by buyer
Countries share a 6-digit HS code and add their own digits for tariffs
HS codes classify services and are not used for physical goods
questions.explain: The HS, run by the World Customs Organization, gives goods a common 6-digit code used for tariffs and trade statistics. Countries add digits for their own tariff lines, such as the 10-digit U.S. HTS.

questions.q: A U.S. exporter will receive EUR 250,000 in 180 days and fears the euro will weaken. Which hedge locks in the dollar value of the receivable?
choices: Sell euros forward for dollars at the 180-day forward rate
Buy euros spot and hold them in a bank account
Buy a euro-denominated bond maturing in 30 days
Raise prices to European customers by 5 percent
questions.explain: A forward sale of euros fixes the future conversion rate. Holding spot euros keeps the currency risk, and a price increase does not guarantee a dollar amount.

questions.q: A currency is quoted at a forward premium against the dollar, meaning its forward rate is above its spot rate. Under covered interest parity, which statement is correct?
choices: The currency is expected to depreciate against the dollar
The currency's interest rates are typically lower than U.S. rates
U.S. interest rates must be lower than the foreign rate
The forward rate must equal the spot rate
questions.explain: A forward premium reflects an interest-rate gap: the currency with the lower interest rate trades at a forward premium against the higher-rate currency.

questions.q: A U.S. importer owes EUR 500,000 in 60 days and expects the euro to appreciate. Which action best hedges the payable?
choices: Delay payment until the euro weakens
Convert dollars to euros now and hold them in a non-interest account
Buy euros forward at the 60-day forward rate
questions.explain: An importer owing euros is short euros, so it buys them forward to fix its dollar cost. Converting early earns no interest and delaying is speculation.

questions.q: The exchange rate moves from USD 1.10 per EUR to USD 1.20 per EUR. What happened to the euro?
choices: The euro depreciated against the dollar
The dollar appreciated against the euro
The euro appreciated against the dollar
The rate is unchanged in real terms
questions.explain: More dollars per euro means each euro buys more dollars, so the euro strengthened.

questions.q: A U.S. firm pays EUR 100,000 for parts. The rate moves from 1.10 to 1.20 USD per EUR. How many more dollars does the firm pay?
questions.explain: EUR 100,000 costs $110,000 at 1.10 and $120,000 at 1.20, a difference of $10,000.

questions.q: A basket of goods costs $5 in the United States and 500 yen in Japan. What is the purchasing power parity exchange rate?
questions.explain: Purchasing power parity sets the rate equal to the price ratio: 500 yen divided by $5 gives 100 yen per dollar.

questions.q: Which is the most accurate definition of a forward exchange rate?
choices: The rate for delivery of currency within two business days
A rate agreed today for exchanging currency on a set future date
The official rate a central bank sets for its currency
The average of daily spot rates over the past year
questions.explain: A forward rate is locked today for a future exchange date, which is why it is used to hedge.

questions.q: A U.S. multinational sends profits from its German subsidiary back to the parent company. What is this called?
questions.explain: Repatriation is moving earnings from a foreign operation to the home country.

questions.q: Which account in the balance of payments records a country's exports and imports of goods and services?
questions.explain: The current account covers trade in goods and services, plus income and transfers. The financial account records investment flows.

questions.q: Which is an example of foreign direct investment?
choices: A U.S. pension fund buys shares of a Japanese company on the Tokyo exchange
A U.S. manufacturer builds a new plant in Mexico that it fully owns
A Canadian bank lends money to a U.S. retailer
An American investor buys U.S. Treasury bonds
questions.explain: FDI means lasting control or a significant stake in a foreign business. Buying shares as a passive investment is portfolio investment.

questions.q: A U.S. firm invoices a Brazilian customer in U.S. dollars, and the real weakens 15 percent before payment. Who bears the currency risk?
choices: The U.S. firm, since its dollar receivable shrinks
Neither party, since the price was fixed in dollars
Both parties equally, since the rate change is shared
The Brazilian customer, who now needs more reais to pay
questions.explain: Invoicing in dollars fixes the seller's receivable, so the buyer carries the exchange risk and must spend more reais. The seller's remaining exposure is indirect: a squeezed customer is more likely to pay late or default.

questions.q: Which situation most clearly describes translation exposure rather than transaction exposure?
choices: A supplier payment due in 30 days in British pounds
A bid on a German contract priced in euros
A subsidiary's balance sheet restated in dollars for consolidation
An import order that has already been paid in yen
questions.explain: Translation exposure arises when foreign-currency financial statements are restated in the parent's currency. Transaction exposure involves actual future cash flows.

questions.q: The exchange rate moves from 18 pesos per dollar today to 20 pesos per dollar six months later. What does this mean for a U.S. firm holding pesos?
choices: The peso weakened, so each peso converts to fewer dollars
The peso strengthened, so each peso converts to more dollars
The dollar weakened against the peso
The peso and dollar are unchanged in value
questions.explain: Needing more pesos per dollar means the peso lost value. A holder of pesos gets fewer dollars for each peso.

questions.q: A U.S. firm licenses its brand to a Korean company for a 6 percent royalty on net sales. Korean net sales are $4,000,000 this year. What royalty does the U.S. firm earn?
questions.explain: 6 percent of $4,000,000 is $240,000. Licensing earns royalties without the firm bearing the investment in production.

questions.q: A firm builds a plant from scratch in Vietnam rather than buying an existing one. Which term fits, and what is its main trade-off?
choices: Acquisition; fast market access but integration risk
Greenfield investment; full control but slower start-up and higher risk
Licensing; little capital needed but less control
Brownfield investment; faster start-up using existing facilities
questions.explain: A greenfield investment builds new facilities, giving control but taking longer and carrying more risk than buying an existing operation.

questions.q: Which entry mode gives the firm the most control but requires the most investment?
questions.explain: A wholly owned subsidiary gives full control of operations and profits, but the firm carries all the investment and risk.

questions.q: Two firms in different countries pool research on one product but remain separate companies. This is best described as:
questions.explain: A strategic alliance is a cooperative agreement between independent firms, with no new legal entity and no ownership transfer.

questions.q: Which entry mode creates a new legal entity jointly owned by a foreign firm and a local partner, sharing profits and control?
questions.explain: A joint venture is a new entity owned by two or more parents, usually used to share risk and gain local knowledge.

questions.q: A U.S. fitness chain wants 200 locations across Southeast Asia within three years while committing little of its own capital. Its value lies in its brand and operating system, and it can enforce standards by contract. Which entry mode fits best?
questions.explain: Franchising lets local owners fund each outlet while paying fees and royalties for the brand and system, so growth is fast and light on capital. Greenfield sites and acquisitions need heavy investment, and contract manufacturing is for making goods, not running service outlets.

questions.q: A firm's entry plan has fixed costs of $600,000 and a contribution margin of $30 per unit. How many units must it sell to break even?
questions.explain: Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit: $600,000 divided by $30 is 20,000.

questions.q: A U.S. firm enters Japan by buying an existing Japanese distributor to gain its channels quickly. Which mode is this, and what is the main risk?
choices: Greenfield; the main risk is slow construction and permits
Licensing; the main risk is low royalty income and weak control
Exporting; the main risk is tariffs and shipping delays
Acquisition; the main risk is overpaying and inheriting hidden liabilities
questions.explain: Acquisitions give quick access but carry valuation and due-diligence risk, including liabilities the buyer did not expect.

questions.q: Which factor most favours a wholly owned subsidiary over a joint venture?
choices: The host country requires a local majority partner
The firm lacks local market knowledge
The firm wants to share start-up costs
Valuable proprietary know-how the firm must protect
questions.explain: Protecting valuable know-how is the main reason to keep full control. The other factors all push toward sharing ownership.

questions.q: A U.S. firm exports to Canada through a distributor that buys the goods outright. Who owns the goods and carries the sales risk?
choices: The U.S. firm, until the goods are sold to end customers
The distributor, once it takes title and pays for the goods
The Canadian end customer, at the port of entry
questions.explain: When a distributor buys outright, title and risk pass to it. Under consignment the exporter keeps title until resale.

questions.q: Which marketing approach uses the same product, message and packaging in every country?
questions.explain: Standardization keeps the marketing mix the same across markets. Adaptation changes it to fit each market.

questions.q: Which Hofstede dimension measures how much less powerful members of a society accept an unequal distribution of power?
questions.explain: Power distance is the degree to which less powerful members accept and expect unequal power. Uncertainty avoidance measures tolerance for ambiguity.

questions.q: Which staffing approach fills key management posts with the parent company's nationals?
questions.explain: An ethnocentric approach relies on home-country nationals for key posts. Polycentric uses host-country managers.

questions.q: Which term describes a home-country employee sent to work abroad?
questions.explain: An expatriate is an employee working outside the country of citizenship, usually sent from headquarters.

questions.q: Which pricing approach sets a low introductory price to gain market share quickly in a new market?
questions.explain: Penetration pricing starts low to win share. Price skimming starts high and lowers the price over time.

questions.q: A product is sold in a foreign market below its home-market price or cost, which may trigger trade remedies. What is this called?
questions.explain: Dumping is selling abroad below normal value. It can lead to antidumping duties if it injures domestic producers.

questions.q: A brand changes its name for Chinese consumers, using characters with a similar sound and a positive meaning. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Localization adapts a product or message to local language and cultural meaning. Standardization keeps it the same everywhere.

questions.q: A U.S. snack brand must reduce sugar and offer vegetarian-friendly flavours in India, while keeping its brand name. Which strategy is this?
choices: Adaptation of the product and marketing mix
questions.explain: Changing the product to meet local tastes and rules, while keeping the brand, is product adaptation.

questions.q: A marketing team runs the same campaign in five countries but adjusts the language and imagery in each. Which term best fits this approach?
questions.explain: Glocalization combines a global core strategy with local adaptation in execution.

questions.q: A U.S. negotiator in Japan finds that counterparts rely on implied meaning, relationships and nonverbal cues more than on explicit wording. This is typical of which kind of culture?
questions.explain: In Edward Hall's model, high-context cultures carry meaning in context, relationships and nonverbal signals, while low-context cultures such as the U.S. rely on explicit words and written terms. Monochronic describes attitudes to time, not communication style.

questions.q: A U.S. toy company is considering entering Mexico. Which step should come first in its global marketing research?
choices: Set prices for the Mexican market
Define the research problem and objectives
questions.explain: The research process starts by defining the problem and objectives. Pricing, distribution and launch decisions depend on that work.

questions.q: A U.S. firm's product sells poorly in a lower-income market even though research shows local buyers like the product, find it easily in stores and recognize the brand. Which element of the 4Ps most likely needs adjustment?
questions.explain: Buyers like the product (product), can find it (place) and know the brand (promotion), which leaves price as the likely barrier in a lower-income market.

questions.q: A product costs $40 per unit to make. The firm wants a 50 percent markup on cost. What is the target price?
questions.explain: A 50 percent markup on $40 adds $20, for a target price of $60.

questions.q: Which description best fits the Hofstede dimension of individualism?
choices: The degree to which people expect to look after themselves and their immediate family
The degree to which people tolerate uncertainty and ambiguity
The degree to which gender roles are clearly separated
The degree to which people focus on long-term rewards
questions.explain: Individualism contrasts with collectivism, where people rely more on group loyalty and extended family.

questions.q: A U.S. sales manager is travelling to meet clients in a country that requires business visitors to get permission to enter, for a stated purpose and length of stay, before arriving. Which document provides that permission?
questions.explain: A visa is the host country's permission to enter for a set purpose and stay, and it is used together with a passport, which proves identity and citizenship. An ATA Carnet covers temporary import of commercial samples, not the traveller.

questions.q: A manufacturer relies on a single Asian supplier for a critical component, holds almost no buffer stock, and a port closure halts production. Which risk is this?
questions.explain: Relying on one supplier with almost no buffer stock leaves the firm exposed to any disruption at a single point. The bullwhip effect is about demand signals growing as they move upstream, not a supply halt.

questions.q: A manufacturer moves some production from China to Mexico to shorten lead times and reduce tariff exposure under USMCA. This is called:
questions.explain: Nearshoring moves production closer to the home market. Reshoring brings it back home, and offshoring moves it farther away.

questions.q: Under which Incoterm does the seller make goods available at its own premises, while the buyer bears all costs and risks from there?
questions.explain: Ex Works (EXW) puts the buyer in charge of export clearance and all transport from the seller's premises, which is the seller's minimum obligation.

questions.q: Under the Incoterms 2020 rule FOB (Free On Board), when does the risk of loss pass from seller to buyer?
choices: When goods arrive at the buyer's warehouse
When goods are loaded on board the vessel at the origin port
When the buyer pays the invoice
When customs clears the goods at the destination
questions.explain: Under FOB, risk passes once the goods are on board the vessel at the named port of shipment. The seller covers costs to that point and the buyer pays the main ocean freight. FOB shipping point is a U.S. domestic (UCC) term, not an Incoterm.

questions.q: Under the Incoterms 2020 rule CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight), which cost does the seller NOT pay?
choices: Ocean freight to the named destination port
Minimum cargo insurance for the voyage
Import duties in the destination country
questions.explain: Under CIF the seller clears the goods for export and pays freight and minimum insurance to the destination port, but import clearance and duties stay with the buyer. Risk passes to the buyer once the goods are on board at the port of shipment.

questions.q: Which practice keeps inventory low by having parts arrive just as they are needed?
questions.explain: Just-in-time inventory delivers materials when needed, which cuts carrying costs but increases dependence on reliable supply.

questions.q: What is the bullwhip effect?
choices: Order variability grows as it moves upstream in a supply chain
Currency values swinging sharply after a trade deal
Tariffs rising in steps over several years
A shipping lane being shut by weather
questions.explain: Small changes in customer demand are amplified as orders move back through distributors, manufacturers and suppliers.

questions.q: A U.S. company uses a freight forwarder to book ocean space and prepare documents. What is the forwarder's main role?
choices: Set the tariff rate on the imported goods
Insure the cargo as the buyer's underwriter
Issue letters of credit for the buyer
Arrange transport and handle shipping documents
questions.explain: Freight forwarders organize transport and paperwork for shippers. They do not set tariffs or issue bank credit.

questions.q: Which document is a receipt for goods shipped and evidence of the contract of carriage?
questions.explain: The bill of lading is issued by the carrier. It is also a document of title that controls who may claim the goods.

questions.q: Which document is the seller's bill to the buyer, stating the goods, quantities and price, and is used for customs valuation?
questions.explain: The commercial invoice is the basic transaction document customs uses to value goods.

questions.q: Which agency administers U.S. economic sanctions programs against certain countries and individuals?
questions.explain: OFAC within the Treasury Department administers and enforces sanctions programs, which bar transactions with designated parties.

questions.q: A government takes over privately owned foreign assets, paying compensation. Which political risk is this?
questions.explain: Expropriation is government seizure of foreign-owned assets. Compensation does not change the classification as a political risk.

questions.q: Which payment is most likely to fall within the FCPA's narrow exception for facilitating payments?
choices: A $25,000 consulting fee to an official who approves permits
A payment to a minister's relative to help win a contract
A gift to a tax judge to reduce a penalty the firm owes
A small fee to a clerk to speed up routine visa processing
questions.explain: The FCPA exempts small facilitating payments that speed up routine, non-discretionary government action, such as processing visas. Payments meant to sway a discretionary decision, like a permit, contract or ruling, are bribes. Canada and the UK ban facilitating payments outright.

questions.q: Which trade remedy offsets a foreign government's subsidy to its exporters?
questions.explain: A countervailing duty offsets subsidies. An antidumping duty offsets sales below fair value.

questions.q: A U.S. firm is planning a large mining investment in a politically unstable country and fears expropriation and civil unrest. Which tool most directly covers those losses?
questions.explain: Political risk insurance, from agencies such as the World Bank's MIGA or private insurers, covers expropriation, currency inconvertibility and political violence. Forward contracts hedge exchange rates, and a confirmed letter of credit secures payment for a sale.

questions.q: Which description best fits ethical relativism in international business?
choices: Ethics are identical in every country
Ethics apply only to home-country laws
Ethics depend only on profit targets
Right and wrong are judged by local cultural norms
questions.explain: Ethical relativism holds that moral standards vary by culture. Critics argue it can excuse practices that are wrong everywhere.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary must follow host-country labour laws even when the parent's home-country standards are higher. Which principle explains this?
choices: Extraterritorial reach of home-country law only
Host-country laws apply to operations within that country
questions.explain: Operations are generally governed by the laws of the country where they take place, though some home-country rules such as the FCPA also apply abroad.

questions.q: Which WTO-permitted measure lets a member temporarily restrict imports when a sudden surge seriously injures a domestic industry?
questions.explain: Safeguards are temporary and non-discriminatory responses to import surges, and they are different from antidumping or countervailing action.

questions.q: Which principle requires that imported goods be treated no less favourably than domestic like goods once they cross the border?
questions.explain: National treatment bars discrimination against foreign goods after entry, including internal taxes and regulations.

questions.q: A firm sets the price of goods sold between its own subsidiaries so that profit shows up in a low-tax country. What is this called?
questions.explain: Transfer pricing sets internal prices, and tax authorities require them to reflect arm's-length values.

questions.q: A subsidiary in Brazil must buy a share of its inputs from local suppliers and reinvest 60 percent of profits locally. What kind of host-government measure is this?
questions.explain: Local content and reinvestment rules are performance requirements that tie market access or operation to specific local actions.

questions.q: Under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), which situation most requires a licence check?
choices: Exporting controlled dual-use technology to a restricted foreign party
Exporting ordinary consumer goods to a retailer in Canada
Shipping published textbooks to a university in France
Sending a printed sales catalogue to a foreign buyer
questions.explain: Dual-use technology sent to restricted parties needs a licence or a licence exception. Routine consumer goods and publications usually do not.

questions.q: A firm learns that its foreign agent has been making payments to customs officials. What is the firm's best immediate step?
choices: Continue the payments, since they are standard in the country
End the agent immediately without any review
Launch an internal investigation with counsel and consider voluntary disclosure
Move the payments to a different subsidiary
questions.explain: Counsel-led investigation and possible voluntary disclosure limit FCPA exposure. Ignoring the problem or moving it does not.

questions.q: Which statement about USMCA rules of origin is correct?
choices: Goods qualify for zero tariffs regardless of where their parts originate
Goods must meet product-specific rules of origin to get preferential tariffs
Any product made in Canada qualifies automatically
Rules of origin apply only to agricultural goods
questions.explain: Each product has a specific origin rule, such as a tariff classification change, a regional value content threshold or both, so simply being assembled in a member country is not enough.

questions.q: A U.S. firm sells to a country whose currency cannot be converted into dollars. Which option best protects its ability to collect payment?
choices: Open account terms with payment due in 90 days
Consignment through a local distributor's warehouse
Cash on delivery paid in the local currency
Countertrade, or a letter of credit confirmed by a U.S. bank
questions.explain: Countertrade avoids converting the currency, and a U.S. bank's confirmation means it pays in dollars even if the buyer's bank cannot transfer funds. Open account, consignment and local-currency cash leave the firm exposed.

vocab.def: A country can produce a good using fewer inputs than another country.
A country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country, so specializing and trading benefits both.
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
A group of countries that removes tariffs among its members while each keeps its own external tariffs.
A free trade area that also adopts a common external tariff toward non-members.
A customs union that also allows free movement of labour and capital among members.
A common market that also harmonizes economic and monetary policy among members.
The obligation to extend any trade advantage given to one trading partner to all WTO members.
The rule that imported goods receive treatment no less favourable than domestic like goods after they enter a market.
A tariff set as a percentage of the declared value of the imported good.
A tariff set as a fixed amount per unit of the imported good, such as dollars per kilogram.
A limit on the quantity or value of a good that may be imported or exported in a period.
A two-tier system with a low tariff on imports within the quota and a higher tariff on imports above it.
A complete government ban on trade with a particular country or in a particular good.
A policy other than a tariff, such as quotas, standards or licensing rules, that restricts trade.
Selling a product in a foreign market below its normal value, usually its home-market price or cost.
A duty imposed on dumped imports to offset the margin of dumping and protect domestic producers.
A duty imposed to offset a subsidy that a foreign government provides to its exporters.
A government payment or benefit that lowers the cost of selling goods abroad.
The standard international product classification system used to assign codes for tariffs and trade statistics.
Standard international trade terms, published by the ICC, that define the seller's and buyer's costs, risks and duties.
An Incoterm under which the seller delivers goods on board the vessel at the origin port and risk passes to the buyer at that point.
An Incoterm under which the seller pays cost, insurance and freight to the named destination port, while risk passes at loading.
An Incoterm under which the seller makes goods available at its own premises and the buyer bears all costs and risks from there.
The seller's bill to the buyer that states the goods, quantities and price, and is used for customs valuation.
A document issued by a carrier that serves as a receipt for goods shipped and evidence of the contract of carriage.
A document that certifies the country where goods were produced, used to determine tariff treatment.
A bank's commitment to pay the seller once compliant shipping documents are presented.
A payment method in which banks handle shipping documents and release them to the buyer only on payment or acceptance, without a bank payment guarantee.
The exchange rate for currency delivered immediately, usually within two business days.
An exchange rate agreed today for exchanging currency on a set future date.
Taking a position, such as a forward contract, that offsets the risk of an existing currency or price exposure.
The theory that exchange rates adjust so that identical goods cost the same across countries.
The part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, net income and net transfers.
Investment that gives a firm lasting control or a significant ownership stake in a foreign business.
Building new facilities from the ground up in a foreign country.
A new entity jointly owned by two or more parent firms that share control, profits and risk.
A foreign business entirely owned and controlled by the parent company.
Granting a foreign firm the right to use intellectual property such as a patent, trademark or technology in exchange for royalties.
A cooperative agreement between independent firms to share resources or skills without creating a new legal entity.
Using the same product, message and marketing mix in every country.
Changing the product or marketing mix to fit the needs and preferences of each local market.
Combining a global core strategy with local adaptation in how it is carried out.
A staffing and management approach that fills key posts with parent-country nationals.
An employee who works in a country other than the one where they hold citizenship, usually sent from headquarters.
The Hofstede dimension measuring how much less powerful members of a society accept unequal distribution of power.
The Hofstede dimension describing the degree to which people look after themselves and immediate family rather than a group.
Setting a low initial price to gain market share quickly in a new market.
A government seizing privately owned foreign assets, with or without compensation.
Coverage that compensates a firm for losses from events such as expropriation, currency inconvertibility or political violence.
A U.S. law that bans bribery of foreign officials to obtain or keep business and requires accurate books and records.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control, which administers and enforces U.S. economic sanctions.
U.S. Commerce Department rules that control exports of dual-use goods, technology and software.
The prices charged between a firm's own units in different countries, which affect where profit and tax are reported.
Moving earnings from a foreign operation back to the parent company's home country.
The amplification of order variability as orders move upstream through a supply chain.
A system that delivers materials as they are needed, reducing inventory but increasing dependence on reliable supply.
Moving production to a nearby country, often to shorten lead times and reduce logistics costs.
Regional value content and origin requirements that goods must meet to receive preferential tariff treatment under USMCA.
The view that moral standards are set by local cultural norms, so the same act may be judged differently in different places.
